Sunday, 9 pm

Week three of the new system, and I finally trust it.

Every evening now has three blocks of ninety minutes: 5 to 6:30, 7 to 8:30, 9 to 10:30. Each block gets one topic, written the night before. There's a chart on my wall with a box for each block. Green tick if done, red cross if not. No half-ticks. Bidisha said that's harsh, but it's honest.

This week: fifteen blocks, twelve green, three red. Organic chemistry twice (I underestimated it), and one physics block I lost to a power cut.

The old me would've just skipped those topics and hoped. Tonight I did the Sunday review instead. I moved all three red topics into next week's plan, first thing Monday and Tuesday, before anything new.

I'm Minakshi, and I feel calmer than I have all year. Nothing is quietly disappearing anymore.

On Saturday afternoon she didn't just look at the score. She took three coloured pens and went through every wrong answer. Red: didn't know the concept. Blue: knew it but made a silly mistake. Black: ran out of time or rushed.

This week: red 4, blue 11, black 3.

"Eleven silly mistakes?" her father, Ramesh, asked, peering at the sheet.

"Mostly signs and units," Irawati said. "So next week isn't more chapters. It's checking."

She planned it on a sticky note: every practice set, underline the unit before answering; last five minutes of every mock, check signs only.

The next Saturday: blue 5.

In January of Class 12, I was sure I'd get computer science at the top engineering college in our state. I'm Minakshi, and I'd never actually checked.

My friend Farida said, "Show your mocks to Mrs. Rao. She's coached students for fifteen years."

So I printed my last four mock scores and the college's closing ranks for the past three years. Mrs. Rao spread them out on the staffroom table and was quiet for a while.

"Computer science there is a stretch," she said. "Not impossible, but a stretch. Your mocks put you around here." She pointed. "But look: electronics and computer engineering at the same college closed here last year. That's realistic."

I felt disappointed for a minute. Then relieved. I had a real target instead of a wish. I kept computer science as my reach option and put the other branch right below it.

The other colleges' deadlines came and went in April and May. Nazia studied and tried not to think about them.

In June, the results came. She'd missed the cutoff by a small margin.

For three weeks she hardly left her room. When she finally looked, most other colleges had closed admissions. One still had a late form, but it needed a portfolio she hadn't prepared. She stayed up four nights in a panic.

Abhinav sat with her on the last night, helping her scan drawings. Neither of them mentioned March.

Rafiq, beta, you didn't clear the cutoff and you think it's over? Listen to your Rekha phuphi. It happened to me.

I was seventeen, in Lucknow. I wanted to study architecture at one famous college. I missed the entrance by a few marks. I cried for a week. My father said nothing. My mother made my favourite food and also said nothing.

Then one evening my father's old friend, Mr. Siddiqui, asked me, "What did you want: the college, or to design buildings?" I said, "To design buildings." He said, "Then let's find the doors."

We found three. A diploma in architecture assistance at the polytechnic, with lateral entry later. A smaller college with a good transfer scheme. Or a retake, but studying differently, with past papers, not just reading.

I did the diploma. Then the degree. I designed schools for thirty years.

qa.a: Three: a diploma, a smaller college with a transfer scheme, or a retake with past papers.

qa.a: The question about the college or designing buildings was the turning point; without it she might have given up on architecture.
